whisper.label: Whisper Large-V3
whisper.text: My interest in stereo photography started when I was about 15 years old in high school. I'd already been interested in photography and started taking three-dimensional pictures with a single camera just by taking a shot and moving slightly and taking another shot and then printing them onto photographic paper and using a simple viewer, stereo viewer to view them with. Stereo photography itself goes back to the beginning of photography when they were first making daguerreotypes in the 1840s and 50s. Records show that the first daguerreotype stereo photographs were made in the late 1840s, early 1850s. It is rather a fascinating history, the way that it evolved and then died. It was a very big thing in the late 1800s because at the time, of course, there was television and radio and people were dying for anything about the rest of the world to be able to see and read about. And these things were extremely popular. This is a home stereoscope that they printed these stereo cards on. And this was the television of the time. Well, I think at the time, anything photographic in the mid-1800s was a fascination. And the introduction of three-dimensional photographs was really huge, very, very huge. And it became very popular for people to make their own at home in the later part of the 19th century with simple box cameras that took black and white slides like this. Really it hasn't been better today, the quality of the photographs that you get from this 1950s technology. Even if you go to an IMAX 3D movie, I think if you look at one of these still color transparencies taken with these 1950s cameras and viewers, it's really hard to imagine a better quality 3D image than what you see with that.
